other.title: Write errors are only logged, so audit data can be lost without anyone noticing

findings.title: Async writer reads the batch after the buffer has emptied it
findings.scenario: flush() passes this.items to write(). write() now only queues the work, and events.map(toLine) runs later inside .then. By then flush() has set items.length = 0 on the same array, so the append writes an empty string. Every audit batch is silently lost.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The old appendFileSync serialized the array before flush() returned. The new writer never copies the array, and no test covers the async path.

findings.title: Write errors are only logged, so audit data can be lost without anyone noticing
findings.scenario: If appendFile fails (disk full or bad path), the batch is dropped and only console.error is called. flushAudit() still resolves normally, so shutdown looks clean.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The catch swallows the rejection, and idle() returns the already-caught promise.

finding.title: Async writer reads the batch after the buffer has emptied it, so audit events are lost

other.title: Write errors are only logged, so failed audit writes are lost without a trace in the caller

findings.title: Async writer reads the batch after the buffer has emptied it, so audit events are lost
findings.scenario: The buffer reaches its batch size and calls write(this.items), then sets items.length = 0 straight away. The writer only reads `events` later, inside .then(() => appendFile(file, events.map(toLine)...)). By then the shared array is empty, so it appends an empty string and every audit batch is silently dropped.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The old appendFileSync consumed the array before the buffer cleared it. The new writer doesn't copy the array, and no test covers the contents of the written file.

findings.title: Write errors are only logged, so failed audit writes are lost without a trace in the caller
findings.scenario: If the disk is full, appendFile rejects. The error goes to console.error, and flushAudit() still resolves normally, so the shutdown path reports success with the batch missing.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The catch swallows the rejection, and idle() returns the already-caught promise.

finding.title: Unset flags pass undefined and overwrite the defaults

findings.title: Unset flags pass undefined and overwrite the defaults
findings.scenario: Running the probe with no flags calls createClient({baseUrl: undefined, retries: undefined, timeoutMs: undefined}). The spread copies those undefined values over DEFAULTS. The URL becomes 'undefined/status'. The loop `attempt <= undefined` is false, so it never calls fetch and then throws `undefined`. AbortSignal.timeout(undefined) would also throw. Passing only --retries 3 breaks baseUrl and timeoutMs the same way.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Spread does not skip keys whose value is undefined. cli.js always sets all three keys, and no test covers the no-flag case.

findings.title: Flag values are not validated: a non-numeric --retries or --timeout becomes NaN
findings.scenario: --retries abc gives NaN, so `attempt <= NaN` is false. The loop never runs and the probe throws undefined. --timeout abc gives NaN, and AbortSignal.timeout(NaN) throws.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Number() does not throw on bad input and nothing checks the result. This is user input, so it needs a check where it enters.

finding.title: Unset flags overwrite defaults with undefined

The probe breaks when no flags are given, so the old defaults are not kept.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Object spread keeps keys whose value is undefined. cli.js passes every key, set or not. No tests exist for this.

findings.title: Non-numeric or invalid --retries/--timeout values are not validated

findings.whyNotPrevented: The flag values are parsed as strings and converted with no check. No tests exist for this.

finding.title: Entries at midnight are counted in two days because entriesBetween includes both ends

other.title: The `to` date is silently excluded from the range

findings.title: Entries at midnight are counted in two days because entriesBetween includes both ends
findings.scenario: A renewal is recorded at 2026-01-02T00:00:00Z, which is what chargeRenewal does through startOfDay. Both the 01-01 row (upper bound inclusive) and the 01-02 row include it. The daily rows and the range total are overstated by that amount.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Ledger.entriesBetween uses `entry.at <= to`. dayStatement avoids this by passing endOfDay (start + DAY_MS - 1). No test covers the report.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/ledger.js:11: `entry.at >= from && entry.at <= to`; src/statement.js uses endOfDay as the upper bound

findings.title: The `to` date is silently excluded from the range
findings.scenario: from=2026-01-01&to=2026-01-31 returns 30 rows and leaves out Jan 31. A caller who expects an inclusive range gets a total that is missing a day. The same call with from=to returns 400.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The endpoint has no documentation or test that states whether `to` is inclusive.

finding.title: Inclusive end bound double-counts entries at UTC midnight

findings.title: Inclusive end bound double-counts entries at UTC midnight
findings.scenario: A renewal is recorded at 2026-01-02T00:00:00Z. The 01-01 query uses [01-01 00:00, 01-02 00:00] and the 01-02 query uses [01-02 00:00, 01-03 00:00]. The entry is counted in both rows, so the range total is overstated. Renewals are always recorded at startOfDay, so this happens for every renewal.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Ledger.entriesBetween uses `entry.at <= to`, so the end is inclusive. statement.js avoids this by passing endOfDay(day), which is the day's last millisecond. No test covers the report.
findings.measuredBy: Grep entriesBetween: src/ledger.js:11 `entry.at >= from && entry.at <= to`; src/renewals.js records `at: startOfDay(periodStart)`

finding.title: Midnight entries are counted in two consecutive days

findings.title: Midnight entries are counted in two consecutive days
findings.scenario: A renewal is recorded at startOfDay(2024-01-02), which is 2024-01-02T00:00:00Z. Ledger.entriesBetween includes both ends (`entry.at <= to`). The entry is counted in the 01-01 row, whose end is 01-02T00:00Z, and again in the 01-02 row. Every renewal is therefore double-counted, and the range total is inflated by the same amount.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Ledger.entriesBetween includes its end. dayStatement avoids this by passing endOfDay (start + DAY_MS - 1). The new code passes the next day's start. No test covers entries at midnight.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/ledger.js: `entry.at >= from && entry.at <= to`. Grep in src/renewals.js: `at: startOfDay(periodStart)`.

findings.title: Range end is exclusive, so a request for the last day omits it
findings.quote: for (let day = startOfDay(from); day < to; day = addDays(day, 1)) {
findings.scenario: A request with from=2024-01-01 and to=2024-01-07 produces rows for 01-01 through 01-06 only. A user asking for a date range expects the `to` day to be included. The route also rejects from == to, so a single day cannot be requested. The error message does not say that `to` is exclusive.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Nothing documents or tests the range semantics. The route check `from >= to` makes the exclusive end the enforced behavior.

finding.title: Rate-limit key uses the raw email, so case or whitespace variants bypass the limit

findings.title: Rate-limit key uses the raw email, so case or whitespace variants bypass the limit
findings.scenario: An attacker makes 5 guesses for victim@x.com, then tries 'Victim@x.com', ' victim@x.com' and 'VICTIM@x.com'. Each variant gets its own counter and its own 5 attempts. UserStore.findByEmail lowercases and trims the email, so all variants resolve to the same account. The 5-per-account limit is bypassed.
findings.whyNotPrevented: UserStore.findByEmail normalizes with normalizeEmail, but the limiter key is built before that and never normalized. No tests cover this.

finding.title: Rate-limit key uses raw email, not the normalized email, so the limit can be bypassed

findings.title: Rate-limit key uses raw email, not the normalized email, so the limit can be bypassed
findings.scenario: The user store looks up accounts with normalizeEmail (trim + lowercase). An attacker guessing passwords for bob@x.com cycles through 'bob@x.com', 'Bob@x.com', 'BOB@x.com', ' bob@x.com' and so on. Each variant gets its own counter but reaches the same account, so the attacker gets far more than 5 attempts per 15 minutes. A non-string body.email also gives a key like 'login:undefined', which is shared by all such requests.
findings.whyNotPrevented: RateLimiter keys on the exact string, and login.js does not call normalizeEmail. No test covers email case variants.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/users.js: findByEmail calls normalizeEmail(email); src/emails.js: normalizeEmail trims and lowercases. src/login.js builds the key from body.email directly.

finding.title: Rate-limit key uses raw email, so case/whitespace variants bypass the per-account limit

findings.title: Rate-limit key uses raw email, so case/whitespace variants bypass the per-account limit
findings.scenario: Attacker sends 5 guesses for 'user@x.com', then 'User@x.com', ' user@x.com', 'USER@x.com', etc. Each variant gets its own counter, but findByEmail normalizes them to the same account. This gives unlimited guesses against one account.
findings.whyNotPrevented: UserStore.findByEmail normalizes via normalizeEmail (src/users.js:13), but the limiter key is built before that and no test covers variants.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/users.js: findByEmail calls normalizeEmail; src/emails.js lowercases and trims. login.js builds the key from body.email unnormalized.

findings.title: Refund moves money from the customer to the store (transfer arguments reversed)
findings.scenario: Refunding a 5000-cent order calls transfer('store', customerId, 5000). The signature is transfer(toAccountId, fromAccountId, amount), so the customer's balance drops by 5000 and the store's rises by 5000. The customer is charged again instead of refunded.
findings.whyNotPrevented: payouts.js passes (seller.accountId, STORE_ACCOUNT), which is the correct order, but nothing checks the order here. The diff adds no tests, and the ledger accepts any account ids.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/ledger.js: `export function transfer(toAccountId, fromAccountId, amountCents)`; src/payouts.js calls transfer(seller.accountId, STORE_ACCOUNT, ...)

findings.title: Partial refunds are not tracked, so repeated refunds can exceed the order total
findings.scenario: A 5000-cent order is refunded 5000 twice. Each call passes the check because it compares only against totalCents. The customer ends up with 10000.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The code stores no record of earlier refunds. The ledger only keeps balances, and no test covers repeated refunds.

findings.title: Refund transfer arguments are reversed, so money moves from the customer to the store
findings.scenario: `transfer` has the signature (toAccountId, fromAccountId, amountCents). This call passes the store as the destination and the customer as the source. Refunding a 5000-cent order debits the customer by 5000 and credits the store by 5000. The customer is charged again and gets no refund.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The arguments are plain strings, so nothing flags the swap. `ledger.js` does not check the direction of a transfer. The diff adds no test for refunds.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/ledger.js: `transfer(toAccountId, fromAccountId, amountCents)` credits the first argument. payouts.js calls `transfer(seller.accountId, STORE_ACCOUNT, ...)`, which has the destination first.

findings.title: Refunds are not tracked, so an order can be refunded repeatedly beyond its total
findings.scenario: Support refunds a 5000-cent order in full, then calls POST /refunds again for the same order, or makes two 3000-cent partial refunds. Each call passes the check against `totalCents` alone, so the customer receives more than the order total.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The check compares only to `order.totalCents`. Nothing records the amount already refunded. The `order` object comes from the request body, so the server cannot rely on it to hold a refunded total.

findings.title: The refund route trusts the order object sent in the request body
findings.scenario: A caller sends an order with an inflated `totalCents` or a different `customerAccountId`. The refund then goes to the wrong account or exceeds the real total.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The handler does not look the order up from a store. No authorization check is visible in the route table. The existing payouts route takes a seller object the same way, so this may be an existing convention.

findings.title: Pressing Enter no longer searches
findings.scenario: The user pastes or autofills a term and presses Enter right away, or types a single character and presses Enter. Submit only calls preventDefault, so no search runs until the debounce fires from an input event. Autofill or a value set without an input event never searches. The author asked for typing to search in addition to Enter, not instead of it.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No test covers the submit path, and the submit handler no longer calls the search.

findings.title: Out-of-order responses can show stale results
findings.scenario: The user types 'sh', then 'shoe'. If the 'sh' response arrives after the 'shoe' response, renderResults overwrites the list with results for 'sh'. Clearing the input to under 2 characters has the same problem: the empty list renders, then a slow earlier response fills it again.
findings.whyNotPrevented: debounce only delays calls. It does not cancel in-flight requests or ignore stale responses. Nothing in search-box.js tracks the latest request.

findings.title: A failed search request becomes an unhandled rejection
findings.scenario: A network error in searchProducts rejects inside the debounced timer callback. Nothing catches it, so the user sees no feedback and the console shows an unhandled rejection. This is lower severity because the old submit handler had the same gap.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The debounce wrapper discards the promise returned by the callback.

findings.scenario: The user types 'sho' and the request starts. They then type 'shoe' and a second request starts. If the 'sho' response arrives after the 'shoe' response, the list shows results for 'sho' while the input says 'shoe'. Debouncing does not cancel requests that are already in flight.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Nothing tracks which request is latest or aborts the earlier one.

findings.title: New minimum term length of 2 was not requested
findings.scenario: A one-character term such as 'a' used to be searchable with Enter. It now clears the results instead.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The author's intent does not mention a minimum length.

findings.title: Out-of-order responses can show results for an older term
findings.scenario: The user types 'shoe', pauses, then types 'shoes'. The 'shoe' request is slower and resolves after the 'shoes' request. renderResults then overwrites the list with results for 'shoe' while the input shows 'shoes'. Debouncing allows more overlapping requests than the old submit-only flow did.
findings.whyNotPrevented: debounce.js only delays calls. Nothing cancels in-flight requests or checks that the term is still current after the await.

findings.title: Undeclared minimum term length of 2 changes behavior
findings.scenario: The user types a single character such as 'x'. The list is cleared and no search runs, where before pressing Enter searched for 'x'. The author only asked for typing-triggered search after a pause.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No test or requirement covers the minimum length. The guard was added on the author's own assumption.

findings.title: Enter no longer triggers an immediate search
findings.scenario: The user types a term and presses Enter within 200ms. Submit does nothing and the user waits for the debounce. Enter also does nothing for a one-character term. The author said the search should happen as the user types 'instead of only' on Enter, which implies Enter should keep working.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The submit handler only prevents the default action and does not call the search.

findings.title: Event for an unknown shipment is acknowledged with 200 and dropped
findings.scenario: A status event arrives for a shipmentId that has not been created yet. updateShipment returns null, the handler still returns 200, and the provider stops retrying. The status update is lost.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The handler ignores updateShipment's return value, and no test covers an unknown id.

findings.title: A signed non-ping event without data throws and the server has no error handling
findings.scenario: A correctly signed event such as {"type":"delivered"} has no data, so event.data.shipmentId throws a TypeError. The handler rejects, and the async request callback in server.js has no try/catch. The request never gets a response, and the unhandled rejection can crash the process on modern Node.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The typedef says data is present on non-ping events, but nothing validates it. server.js does not catch handler errors.

other.title: A signed non-ping event without `data` throws and nothing catches it

findings.title: A signed non-ping event without `data` throws and nothing catches it
findings.scenario: A correctly signed body such as `{"type":"in_transit"}`, or the JSON literal `null`, makes `event.data.shipmentId` or `event.type` throw a TypeError. The server's async request callback has no catch, so the rejection is unhandled. On Node 15 and later that crashes the process, and the provider keeps retrying the event.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The ShippingEvent typedef says `data` is absent only on ping, and the handler does no shape check after JSON.parse. server.js wraps the handler call in no try/catch. The signature check limits who can trigger this to the provider or someone holding the secret, so the risk is low.

findings.title: Writes saved values into the shared defaults object
findings.scenario: defaultPreferences() returns the module-level DEFAULT_PREFERENCES, not a copy. User A has saved theme 'dark'. Fetching A overwrites the global default with 'dark'. User B has no saved theme, and fetching B returns theme 'dark'. Preferences leak between users, and the defaults stay changed until the process restarts.
findings.whyNotPrevented: defaults.js returns the same object on every call. Nothing freezes or copies it, and the diff has no tests.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/defaults.js: `return DEFAULT_PREFERENCES;` returns the shared constant

findings.title: `in` check also matches inherited property names
findings.scenario: Saved JSON containing a key such as "toString" or "constructor" passes the `in` check, because it exists on the prototype. The unsupported key is then written onto the result. A saved "__proto__" key would replace the object's prototype.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` checks the prototype chain. Nothing restricts the keys to own properties.

findings.title: Shared defaults object is mutated, so one user's preferences leak into every other user
findings.scenario: User A has savedPreferences {theme:'dark'}. preferencesFor(A) writes 'dark' into the module-level DEFAULT_PREFERENCES. User B has no saved preferences, and GET /users/B now returns theme 'dark' instead of 'light'. The change persists for the life of the process.
findings.whyNotPrevented: defaultPreferences() in src/defaults.js returns the DEFAULT_PREFERENCES constant itself, with no copy and no freeze. No test covers two consecutive calls.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/defaults.js: `return DEFAULT_PREFERENCES;` returns the shared constant, and preferencesFor assigns `preferences[key] = value` on it.

findings.title: `key in` also matches inherited keys such as constructor, toString and __proto__
findings.scenario: savedPreferences is parsed from JSON, so it can contain an own key like "constructor" or "__proto__". `in` returns true for those keys, so the code writes them onto the preferences object. An unsupported key then ends up in the response, or the object's prototype gets replaced, instead of the key being ignored.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` checks the prototype chain. Nothing restricts the saved keys to the supported ones.
